Series::fmax¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::fmax(const Series& other) const

Selecting A Maximum Without Letting Missing Values Win¶

fmax() compares two series element by element and returns the larger value. Its defining rule is what happens when one candidate is NaN: the numeric candidate wins. A result is NaN only when both candidates are NaN.

This makes fmax() useful when NaN means “no observation” rather than “the whole calculation is invalid.” For example, two sensors may cover different parts of a grid. left.fmax(right) keeps the strongest available reading at each location without requiring a separate missing-value mask.

This is a pairwise transform, not a reduction. It does not find one maximum for the whole receiver, and it does not remove dimensions. The result has the broadcast shape of the two operands.

Choosing Between fmax() And maximum()¶

Use fmax() when a lone NaN should behave like a missing candidate. Use maximum() when any NaN should mark the result invalid. On integer data, and on floating data without NaN, the two methods agree.

Parameters¶

other (const Series&): the competing values. Trailing dimensions follow the normal broadcasting rules. The two series must be on the same platform. Complex inputs are rejected because complex numbers have no total ordering.

Returns¶

A new Series with the broadcast shape and promoted dtype. Neither input is modified. There is no public in-place fmax_() member.

Gradient¶

Sensitivity follows the value selected in the forward pass. The larger finite operand receives the upstream sensitivity and the smaller receives zero. A finite tie is symmetric, so each operand receives half. If exactly one operand is NaN, the numeric operand receives all of the sensitivity.

Examples¶

1. Missing values lose the comparison¶

const double nan = std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN();
auto left  = pluss::make_series({1.0, nan, 4.0, nan});
auto right = pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0, 4.0, nan});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, left.fmax(right));

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[2.0000, 3.0000, 4.0000, nan]

The second lane takes 3 because it is the only numeric candidate. The final lane remains NaN because neither side supplies a number.

2. Reverse routing includes ties and missing lanes¶

const double nan = std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN();
auto a = pluss::make_series({1.0, 4.0, 3.0, nan});
auto b = pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0, nan, 5.0});
a.tracks_slope_(true);
b.tracks_slope_(true);

a.fmax(b).sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.sensitivity()) << '\n';
pluss::series::print(std::cout, b.sensitivity());

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 0.5000, 1.0000, 0.0000]
Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, 0.5000, 0.0000, 1.0000]

Read the columns vertically: b wins lane 0; lane 1 is tied; a is the only number in lane 2; and b is the only number in lane 3.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Both-NaN still produces NaN; this method skips missing candidates but does not invent replacements.

  • Infinity is an ordinary ordered value. +inf wins a maximum and -inf loses it.

  • Broadcasting can enlarge the result. Inspect the operand shapes when a pairwise comparison unexpectedly returns more elements.

  • There is no scalar overload. Use a one-element Series, or use clamp_min() when the intent is a fixed lower bound.

See Also¶

  • Series::fmin: select the smaller available value.

  • Series::maximum: propagate NaN instead of skipping it.

  • Series::amax: reduce one or more dimensions to maxima.
